proposal: I would like to remove the silver birch tree that is in our small garden. It is the only tree there. The tree is NOT subject to a TPO, but the house is in a conservation area, so we need permission. We have had (and used) permission from the council in the past to carry out crown reduction of this same tree (a silver birch), but the tree is getting bigger and thicker, and more problematical to deal with. This means that it is less attractive, and less silver than it used to be. But more importantly, and the reason for this application, its roots are starting to cause damage. I attach pictures of the damage that it has done to our garden wall. The tree is also reasonably close to Ednam House, which is a council owned block, and it is foreseeable that in the future it would cause damage or difficulty to those premises, which would of course, cause difficulties for the residents and, at least indirectly, the council. Also, since the tree has grown bigger, its foliage interferes with the light (which comes from the south up Florence Road and across Upper Tollington Park, which will mean that many of the flats in Ednam House are overshadowed by tree foliage and gloomier than the residents might wish. We are also very close to the Parkland Walk, and there are trees on Florence Road, so the utility of this tree is less than it might be in a less arboreal neighbourhood. For that reason, although we have tried to look after it, we strongly feel that the utility both for ourselves and our neighbours is the tree's removal. I have not (yet) instructed a surveyor or other professional to assess this, since the risk of damage is clear and the damage that it has caused is visible in the photographs. Essentially, despite intervention, the tree is growing too big, is less attractive than it once was and is causing damage to property, as well as making the garden more difficult to cultivate and use for other beneficial purposes. I attach a number of photographs. Obviously, we would instruct skilled professionals to remove the tree were permission granted. We have used appropriately licensed and regulated tree surgeons to do the crown reduction works in the past.

Structural Hazard to Adjacent Window Bay: The tree exhibits a severe, unnatural trunk lean angled directly toward the adjacent residential window bay. During high wind events, dynamic sail-loading (compounded by heavy ivy) creates continuous leverage on the slender trunk, posing an imminent risk of failure into habitable rooms. 2. Inadequacy of Previous Pruning (Ref: HGY/2026/2273): Approval under HGY/2026/2273 pruned branches to 2m clearance, but failed to resolve the primary hazard: the structural lean of the main trunk toward the windows. 3. Documented Branch Failures & Active Structural Instability: The tree has a documented history of branch failure, with fallen branches already recorded on site. This active shedding demonstrates structural weakness within the crown canopy, which—when combined with heavy foliage and dense ivy—creates dynamic sail-loading and excessive leverage on an already leaning trunk. 4. Structural Hazard & Direct Proximity: The severe, unnatural trunk lean is angled directly toward the adjacent residential window bay. Given the history of branch drop and the trunk’s angle, high wind events pose an imminent, unacceptable risk of major structural failure into habitable rooms. 5. Request for Site Visit: Report HGY/2026/2273 noted no site visit was conducted. An in-person assessment is requested to evaluate the trunk angle and structural proximity to the window bay. 6. Low Amenity: The tree is not publicly visible and holds minimal amenity value relative to the risk to adjacent windows. While pollarding or pruning was previously considered, it is no longer a viable or safe solution for this specific tree. Previous pruning (Ref: HGY/2026/2273) failed to address the core problem: a severe, fundamental structural lean of the main trunk directly toward the residential window bay. Pruning does not correct root plate instability or prevent the leaning trunk from failing under heavy wind loads. We actively welcome and request an in-person site visit by a Haringey Tree Officer to verify the severe trunk angle and structural risk to the window bay, addressing previous concerns regarding assessments (if applicable).
